opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it surprised us too. Going in, cable management was near the top of our list of things we thought would bite us. You picture a robot moving around a factory floor, tethered to power, and you imagine it wrapping itself around a table leg or snagging on a cart within the first hour.

In practice, a few things worked in our favor. The biggest one is that factory work is far more structured than people assume. These robots aren't wandering around. They do a fairly bounded set of motions in a fairly bounded workspace, often at one station or along a short, predictable path. Once you know the envelope the robot operates in, you can route the cable so it stays out of that envelope. Overhead festooning or a simple boom does a lot of the work, so the cable comes down from above rather than trailing along the floor where things can catch it.

The second thing is that the robot can just be aware of its own tether. It knows where it's been and how much it has turned, so you can build in a simple rule: don't keep rotating in the same direction, unwind when you get a chance. It's almost trivially cheap to track compared with the hard perception and manipulation problems we're solving anyway.

Third, the factories themselves helped. These are environments that already deal with hoses, air lines, and powered tools every day. The people on the floor know how to run cable safely, and they gave us good feedback early on about where things should and shouldn't go.

So the lesson for us was that the problem we feared in the abstract turned out to be a fairly solvable engineering detail once we were in real deployments. The genuinely hard problems were elsewhere: reliability over long shifts, handling variation in parts, and recovering gracefully when something unexpected happens. Being tethered actually bought us something too. You don't have battery swaps or charging downtime, and in a factory running multiple shifts, that matters a lot.

r001.rationale: It says the robots follow bounded motions in predictable workspaces, making it possible to route cables outside their movement envelope.

r002.rationale: It mentions tracking turns and unwinding, but does not identify moving backward instead of turning around as a way to prevent tangling.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was one of those things we spent way too much time worrying about in the planning phase. When you watch a tethered robot move around a factory floor, your mental model is this nightmare of cable spaghetti, and we'd budgeted a lot of engineering time for active cable management, like motorized reels, slack sensors, all that.

What we found in deployment was that the problem mostly solves itself if you're disciplined about two much simpler things. First, the robot's workspace is far more constrained than you imagine. In a real factory cell, the robot isn't wandering; it's moving between a handful of stations along pretty repeatable paths. So the cable sees the same motion over and over. Once you route it with a fixed anchor point overhead and a bit of a service loop, it just finds a steady state. It doesn't accumulate twist the way it would if the robot were freely roaming.

Second, we constrained the robot's base rotation in software. We just didn't let it spin more than about three hundred degrees in one direction before unwinding. That's a trivial rule to implement, and it eliminated the one failure mode that actually causes tangling, which is cumulative rotation. Nobody notices the robot taking the long way around once in a while.

So the lesson for us was that the exotic hardware solution was addressing a problem we were imagining in an unconstrained environment. The real environment had structure we could exploit. I think that pattern comes up a lot in robotics: the thing that terrifies you in simulation turns out to be mundane on the floor, and the thing that bites you is something boring, like a connector working loose from vibration.

r001.rationale: The response says the robots move among a handful of stations on repeatable paths, so their limited, structured movement helps the cable settle without accumulating twist.

r002.rationale: It describes limiting base rotation and unwinding after about 300 degrees, but does not say the robots move backward instead of turning around.

In a factory, they’re generally repeating a task in a defined area, so you can plan where the power cable runs and keep it out of their path. It sounds like a big problem when you imagine a robot going anywhere, but with that constrained movement, it’s much more manageable.

r001.rationale: It says factory robots repeat tasks in a defined area, making their movement constrained and cable routing manageable.

sol-6.1.text: We initially thought cable management was going to be a big challenge. But in a factory, the robot is generally doing a repetitive task in a defined area. It isn’t wandering around and turning in random directions. Once you understand that motion and route the power cable around it, avoiding tangles becomes pretty straightforward.
